Title: ISO 24508:2019 Ergonomics - Accessible design - Guidelines for designing tactile symbols and characters
Research area: Tactile symbol and character legibility standard
Problem addressed: Need for internationally agreed physical parameters for touch-readable symbols on products, facilities and packaging.
Target population: People who need non-visual information, incl. older people; covers products, housing, transport, packaging.
Methodology: Consensus standard (ergonomics committee); not an empirical study.
Technology: Convex (raised) tactile symbols and characters read by fingers; excludes Braille, vibratory/temporal patterns.
Main findings: Clause 4.3: symbol size >= 10 mm (except dots/lines); character size >= 15 mm; x1.5 sizes for older people unaccustomed to tactile symbols; dots/bars per ISO 24503; when dots and bars are mixed, dot diameter < 1.5 mm and bar length > 5 mm. Clause 4.4: line width about 1/10 of symbol size, within 0.5-3.0 mm. Clause 4.5: raised height 0.3-1.5 mm. Spacing must be 'sufficient' (note cites ANSI A117.1 and DIN 32986 values). Recommends simple geometric shapes, filled or outlined; symbols should have a fixed common meaning (example: triangle on toxic-substance packaging, ISO 11683); dotted/broken lines are not used as symbol components.
Limitations: Paywalled full text; cross-sectional profile requirements (4.6) not verified; no switch-specific guidance found in preview.
Research gaps: No guidance on assigning meanings to symbols for electrical controls (light/fan/socket).
Relevance to SPARSH: Primary numeric source for SPARSH cap symbols (size, line width, height).
Design implications: Cap symbol >= 10 mm (>= 15 mm for older users); line width 1-1.5 mm for a 10-15 mm symbol; relief 0.5-1.5 mm (stay within 0.3-1.5 mm); note the triangle already carries a 'danger' meaning on packaging (ISO 11683) - consider whether triangle = socket could be read as a hazard cue (arguably appropriate for a socket, but should be tested).

Title: Guidelines for Standardizing the Design of Tactile Maps: A Review of Research and Best Practice
Authors: Jakub Wabinski; Albina Moscicka; Guillaume Touya
Problem addressed: Tactile map guidelines are scattered, conflicting and little known; slows production.
Target population: Researchers and practitioners producing tactile maps; end users are people with VI.
Methodology: Critical review building on ~600-study prior systematic review plus non-systematic Scopus/WoS search; practitioner questionnaire (8 responses, 7 countries).
Technology: Swell paper, thermoforming, vacuum forming, 3D printing.
Main findings: Prefer simplest recognisable shapes; outline symbols easier than filled; semicircular/trapezoidal cross-sections rather than square; simple geometric point symbols (circle, square, triangle) most common; limit to ~10-15 symbols per map. Numeric table: point symbol 3-6 mm typical (ISO 2019: 10 mm); min gap between different symbols 1-5 mm; min gap around 3D point symbols 1 cm (Holloway et al. 2019); min symbol height 0.2-0.75 mm across sources, optimal 0.3-1.5 mm (ISO 2019); same-shape symbols need 25-30% size difference; Wiedel & Groves: Braille 0.5 mm, lines 1 mm, points 1.5 mm.
Limitations: Non-systematic search; tiny practitioner sample; values conflict and often omit production method; many sources are 1950s-1970s; no Braille dot numbers.
Research gaps: Calls for global standards and testing with people with VI; little on 3D-printed objects for controls.
Relevance to SPARSH: Provides the cross-source numeric table SPARSH can cite for symbol size, spacing and height; supports circle/triangle/line as canonical tactile primitives.
Design implications: Use rounded (semicircular/trapezoidal) edges, not sharp square profiles; keep >= 3 mm (ideally more) between distinct raised elements; avoid confusable same-shape sizes (needs 25-30% difference).

Title: ISO 24503:2011 Ergonomics - Accessible design - Tactile dots and bars on consumer products
Research area: Tactile marking of controls on consumer products
Problem addressed: Need consistent tactile marks on product controls.
Target population: Everyone incl. older persons and persons with disabilities; personal-use products.
Main findings: Dot diameter 0.8-2.0 mm, height 0.4-0.8 mm; bar width 0.8-2.0 mm, length 5-10x width, height 0.4-0.8 mm. Conventions: DOT on the control that starts a major function / power ON; BAR on stop/cancel; an ON/OFF toggle gets only a dot; dot on 'increase' side; place marks on the control itself or adjacent stationary surface; keep clear of braille.
Limitations: Excludes other symbols (triangles, squares) and textures; paywalled.
Research gaps: No convention for denoting what an electrical switch controls.
Relevance to SPARSH: IMPORTANT CONFLICT: SPARSH uses dot = light and line = fan, but ISO 24503 assigns dot = start/ON and bar = stop/cancel. Users familiar with ISO-marked appliances could misread a SPARSH 'line' cap as 'off/stop'.
Design implications: Either (a) justify and test the current code, or (b) choose SPARSH shapes that avoid ISO dot/bar meanings (e.g., keep circle/triangle, replace dot/line with other distinct shapes), or (c) place function shapes on the cap top and reserve a small ISO dot for the ON side of the rocker.

Title: Size and Spacing of Braille Characters
Problem addressed: Braille dimensions vary between paper and signage specifications.
Main findings: NLS Specification 800 (paper): dot height 0.019 in (0.48 mm), base diameter 0.057 in (1.44 mm), dot spacing 0.092 in (2.34 mm), cell spacing 0.245 in (6.2 mm). ANSI A117.1-2003 (signage): base 1.5-1.6 mm, height 0.6-0.9 mm, dot spacing 2.3-2.5 mm, cell spacing 6.1-7.6 mm, line spacing 10.0-10.2 mm. California Title 24: dot height min 0.635 mm.
Relevance to SPARSH: Reference values if SPARSH adds braille numbers/letters to caps or the legend card.
Design implications: If braille is added, use signage values (dot height 0.6-0.9 mm, base 1.5-1.6 mm, domed).

Title: 2010 ADA Standards for Accessible Design, Section 703.3 Braille (Table 703.3.1)
DOI/URL: https://www.access-board.gov/ada/ (official); text read via corada.com mirror of 703.3
Problem addressed: Regulatory dimensions for braille on signs.
Main findings: Dot base diameter 1.5-1.6 mm; dot height 0.6-0.9 mm; dot spacing 2.3-2.5 mm; adjacent cells 6.1-7.6 mm; rows 10-10.2 mm; dots shall be domed or rounded.
Relevance to SPARSH: Confirms domed profile and 0.6-0.9 mm height for any braille on SPARSH legend/caps.
Design implications: Domed/rounded profiles for all raised features (also matches Facade's switch from cylinders to domes).

Title: JIS S 0052:2024 Accessible design - Guidelines for designing tactile symbols and characters
Authors: Japanese Industrial Standards Committee / Japanese Standards Association (drafted by AIST)
Journal/conference: Japanese Industrial Standard (revision of JIS S 0052:2011)
Target population: Users relying on touch; covers home appliances, housing equipment, packaging.
Main findings: Based on ISO 24508:2019 with Japan-specific technical changes; covers home appliances explicitly; Annex JA on dot/line tactile textures (no ISO counterpart). Numeric values not visible in preview.
Relevance to SPARSH: Shows ISO 24508 is applied to home appliances nationally; India has no equivalent.
